lessons.title: Study Session 1: Who Is Actually Reading This

blocks.text: Introduction

Zainab Lawal used to write every workplace document the same way she once wrote university essays, for a reader who already agreed with her and had unlimited time to read closely. This session teaches you to picture the actual person who will read what you write, and to let that picture shape every choice you make before you draft a single sentence.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Explain why writing without a clear reader in mind usually fails its purpose. e Identify what a specific reader already knows and needs from a document. e State a document's purpose in one sentence before drafting.
e Adjust a draft when you realise you wrote for yourself instead of the reader. 2.0 Main Content
A Memo Nobody Finished Reading

Zainab Lawal coordinates procurement for a manufacturing supplier in Abuja, and her first major memo to the finance team, a request to approve a new vendor, ran to two and a half pages of careful background before it ever stated what she actually wanted approved. Her manager stopped her in the hallway two days later, not to discuss the vendor, but to ask what the memo had actually been asking for. Nobody on the finance team had read past the first page.
Writing as a Conversation With Someone Specific

In 1981, the researchers Linda Flower and John Hayes published a study in College Composition and Communication describing what skilled writers actually do differently from less skilled ones. Their finding was clear: strong writers hold an active mental picture of their reader and their own purpose throughout the entire writing process, planning, drafting and revising with that reader constantly in mind, while weaker writers tend to write from their own point of view first and only adjust for the reader afterward, if at all, usually just at the level of individual sentences.
Building the Picture Before Writing

Naming What the Reader Already Knows A reader who already understands the background does not need it repeated in full, and a reader who does not will be lost without it; naming, before writing, exactly what this specific reader already knows saves both the wasted explanation and the confusing gap.
Naming What the Reader Actually Needs From This Document

A document exists to make something happen, an approval, a decision, an action, and naming that outcome in one plain sentence before drafting keeps every paragraph afterward pointed toward it rather than toward general background.

Checking Whether the Draft Still Serves the Reader Rereading a finished draft specifically from the reader's position, not the writer's, often reveals sections that exist because the writer needed to think them through, not because the reader needs to read them.
Key Practices

e¢ Name what your specific reader already knows before drafting. e State your document's purpose in one sentence before writing further. e Write toward the outcome you actually need, not toward general background.
e Reread a finished draft from the reader's position before sending it.
A Worked Example: Zainab's Memo, Before and After

Zainab's original memo opened with a full history of the company's vendor relationships going back three years, useful context she herself had needed to gather, but not information the finance team lacked or needed repeated. The actual request, approval for a new vendor at a specific cost, did not appear until the final paragraph of the second page.

Her revised memo opens with one sentence: | am requesting approval to onboard Vendor X at a monthly cost of 400,000 naira, replacing our current supplier. The background that follows is three sentences, not three paragraphs, included only because it answers a question the finance team would otherwise have to ask. The memo is now half a page long, and it was approved the same afternoon it was sent.
Common Pitfalls

Writing everything the writer herself needed to understand a topic, rather than what the reader actually needs to act on it, is the mistake beginners make most often at this stage. A document written to prove the writer did her homework, rather than to help the reader decide something, usually buries its real point under material that belonged in the writer's own notes, not in the finished document.
The Reader Was There the Whole Time

Zainab's memos have not become shorter because she stopped thinking carefully. They have become shorter because she now does that careful thinking before she writes, not on the page the reader has to read through.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to hold a clear picture of your reader and purpose before drafting, rather than writing from your own point of view first. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where the same discipline shapes how you write a professional email that actually gets answered.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Think of a recent document you wrote. What did your reader already know that you explained anyway?
2. State the actual purpose of one document you need to write soon, in a single sentence, before you draft it. Practical Output: Practical Output
One real workplace document rewritten with its purpose stated in the first sentence and unnecessary background removed.
References and Further Reading
e Flower, L., & Hayes, J.R. (1981). A cognitive process theory of writing. College Composition and Communication, 32(4), 365 to 387.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 15:23, on the joy in an apt answer, and how good a timely word is.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Ibrahim 14:4, on every messenger being sent speaking the language of his own people, to make things clear to them.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: The Email That Gets Answered

blocks.text: Introduction

Patrick Oduya used to write emails the way he would tell a story out loud, building up to the point slowly, certain his reader would stay with him the whole way. This session teaches you to write for how people actually read on a screen, so your point survives even a reader who only skims the first few lines.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
e Structure an email so its purpose is visible without scrolling.
e Write a subject line that states the actual ask.
e Front-load the most important information rather than building up to it. e Format an email for fast, partial reading.
¢ Close an email with a clear, specific action. 2.0 Main Content
Buried in the Third Paragraph

Patrick Oduya manages logistics scheduling for a distribution company in Nairobi, and for months his emails to drivers and warehouse staff went unanswered or were answered incorrectly, not because his information was wrong, but because his actual request usually appeared in the third paragraph, after two paragraphs of context. Colleagues skimmed the first few lines, saw nothing urgent, and moved on before reaching the part that needed areply.
How People Actually Read a Screen

In 2006, the usability researcher Jakob Nielsen published the results of an eyetracking study following 232 users across thousands of web pages, finding that people read on screen in a consistent F-shaped pattern, a full first line, a shorter second line, and then a scan down the left edge of the remaining text, rather than reading every word in order. The first line of any message receives far more attention than anything that follows it, which means a message that saves its real point for later is often never read in full at all.
Writing for the F-Shaped Reader

A Subject Line That States the Ask A subject line that names the actual request, Approval needed by Friday, Vendor X onboarding, is answered faster than a vague one, Question, because a reader can prioritise it correctly before even opening the message.
Putting the Point in the First Line

The most important sentence in any email belongs at the very top, before any greeting-level pleasantries expand into background, since the first line is read by nearly everyone who opens the message, even those who read no further.

Formatting for a Partial Read Short paragraphs, a bolded key phrase, and a clear line break between the ask and the supporting detail let a reader who only skims still catch the essential point, rather than losing it inside a dense, unbroken block of text.
Key Practices
e Write a subject line that states the actual request.
e Put your most important sentence first, not buried in later paragraphs.
e Break long explanations into short paragraphs a skimming reader can still follow. © Close with one clear, specific action, not a vague sign-off.
e Reread your own email as if you only had five seconds to find the point.
A Worked Example: Patrick's Email, Before and After

Patrick's old email to warehouse staff about a delayed delivery began, | hope this finds you well. As you may recall, last month's shipment schedule was adjusted due to the rainy season, and this has had some knock-on effects this week. The actual point, that Thursday's delivery would arrive four hours late and staff needed to adjust the unloading schedule, appeared in the fourth sentence of the second paragraph.

His revised email opens: Thursday's delivery will arrive four hours late, at approximately 2pm. Please adjust the unloading schedule accordingly. The context that follows is two short sentences, clearly separated, for anyone who wants the reason. Staff began replying to confirm within minutes rather than missing the message entirely.
Common Pitfalls

Beginners at this stage often assume a reader will read an entire email carefully simply because it was sent to them, when in practice most workplace email is skimmed, not read, and any message that depends on a reader reaching the third paragraph will fail for a meaningful share of its recipients.
Five Seconds Is Usually All You Get

Patrick's emails are not shorter because he has less to say. They are structured so the part that matters most survives even the five seconds most colleagues actually give a message before deciding whether to keep reading.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to write emails for how people actually read on a screen, front-loading the point and formatting for a partial read. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where the same discipline shapes how you structure a longer workplace report.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Look at a recent email you sent. Where did your actual point appear, and would a five-second reader have found it?
2. Rewrite one email subject line so it states the actual request rather than a vague topic. Practical Output: Practical Output
One real email rewritten with a specific subject line, the main point in the first sentence, and short, skimmable paragraphs.
References and Further Reading
¢ Nielsen, J. (2006). F-Shaped Pattern for Reading Web Content (original eyetracking research). Nielsen Norman Group.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Habakkuk 2:2, on writing the vision and making it plain so a reader may run with it.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Bagarah 2:282, on writing down a matter clearly and justly between parties.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: A Report That Holds Its Shape

blocks.text: Introduction

Rahel Tesfaye writes monthly field reports for an NGO in Asmara, often late at night after helping her aging mother settle in for the evening, and she cannot afford a report that takes longer to write or read than it needs to. This session teaches you to structure a report so its shape carries the reader, rather than asking the reader to build that shape herself.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
¢ Distinguish a report's purpose from a narrative account of events.
¢ Open a report with its main conclusion rather than building toward it. e Organise supporting detail under clear, predictable headings.
e Separate fact from recommendation within a report.
e Match a report's length to its actual audience and purpose.
e Check a draft report against a plain-language standard before submitting it. 2.0 Main Content
A Report Told Like a Story

Rahel's early field reports read like a diary of her month, what she visited, in what order, what she noticed along the way, ending with a conclusion that a reader had to wait until the final page to reach. Her programme director valued the information deeply and still asked her, gently, after the third such report, to lead with what she actually needed the head office to know or decide.
A Standard Built for Clarity, Not Decoration

In 2011, the Plain Language Action and Information Network, a working group across United States federal agencies, published the Federal Plain Language Guidelines, a practical standard for writing documents that state their main point early, organise information around what a reader needs, and are tested against how real readers actually use them. Their central recommendation for reports and other official documents is direct: open with the bottom line, the main conclusion or request, before the supporting detail that led there, because a reader who has to search for the point is a reader who may never find it.
A Shape a Reader Can Rely On
Leading With the Bottom Line

A report's first paragraph should state its main finding or recommendation plainly, three villages now have functioning water access following this month's repairs, rather than opening with the sequence of the writer's own month.
Organising Under Predictable Headings
Consistent headings, Summary, Findings, Recommendations, let a reader who needs only one section find it immediately, rather than reading the full report to locate the part relevant to her.
Keeping Fact and Recommendation Visibly Separate

A reader needs to know clearly which statements are observed fact and which are the writer's judgement about what should happen next; blending the two makes it hard for a reader to evaluate either one on its own terms.
Key Practices

e Open a report with its main conclusion, not a chronological account. e Use consistent, predictable headings so a reader can find what she needs quickly. e Keep factual findings visibly separate from recommendations.
e Match the report's length to what the audience actually needs, not to how much happened.
A Worked Example: Rahel's Report, Before and After

Rahel's original report for March ran four pages, moving chronologically from her first site visit to her last, with the actual outcome, that water access had been restored to three villages while a fourth remained delayed pending a part delivery, appearing only in the final paragraph.

Her revised report opens with a two-sentence summary stating exactly that outcome. A Findings section follows with the specific, dated evidence supporting it. A separate Recommendations section proposes an expedited part order for the fourth village, clearly marked as her judgement rather than an observed fact. The report is now two pages long, and her programme director reads the summary alone for most months, going deeper only when something requires it.
Common Pitfalls

Writing a report as a chronological account of the writer's own month, rather than as an answer to the question a reader actually has, is the error that costs new report writers the most rework. A reader forced to reconstruct the main point from a sequence of events is a reader who may act on an incomplete or incorrect understanding of what actually happened.
A Shape That Respects the Reader's Time
Rahel's reports have not become less thorough. The same detail is still there, organised now so a reader can take exactly as much of it as she needs, in exactly the order she needs it.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to structure a report around its conclusion and clear headings, rather than a chronological account. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where the same respect for the reader's time shapes how you edit a document down to what matters.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Look at a report you have written or received recently. Did it open with its main point, or did the reader have to search for it?
2. Rewrite the opening of one report you know well as a two-sentence bottom-line summary. Practical Output: Practical Output
One report opening rewritten as a two-sentence bottom-line summary, followed by findings and recommendations organised under separate headings.
References and Further Reading
e Plain Language Action and Information Network (2011). Federal Plain Language Guidelines. Washington, DC: PLAIN.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Luke 1:3, on writing an orderly, carefully investigated account.
e Qur'an, Surah Al-Isra 17:36, on not pursuing what one has no knowledge of, since hearing, sight and heart will all be questioned.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Zainab's finance team did not read past the first page of her memo. What was the underlying cause?
options: The memo used incorrect grammar
The memo buried its actual request under two pages of background the reader did not need repeated
The finance team was too busy to read any memo
The memo was too short
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Flower and Hayes's 1981 research, what do skilled writers do differently from less skilled writers?
options: They write faster
They hold an active mental picture of their reader and purpose throughout the writing process
They avoid revising their work
They use longer sentences
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend naming before drafting a document?
options: The writer's own opinion only
What the specific reader already knows and what the document needs to achieve
The longest possible background explanation
Nothing, drafting should begin immediately
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

quiz.q: Patrick's emails to drivers and warehouse staff often went unanswered. What was the actual cause, according to this session?
options: His information was consistently wrong
His actual request usually appeared in the third paragraph, after readers had stopped reading
Colleagues did not have email access
His emails were too short
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Nielsen's 2006 eyetracking study, how do people typically read on a screen?
options: Word by word, in complete order, every time
In an F-shaped pattern, with the first line receiving far more attention than later text
From the bottom of the page upward
They do not read screens differently from printed pages
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

quiz.q: What makes a subject line effective, according to this session?
options: Vagueness, so the reader is curious enough to open it
Stating the actual request so the reader can prioritise it correctly
Length, the longer the better
Including as many topics as possible in one line
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Cutting It Down to What Matters

blocks.text: Introduction

Aminata Diarra used to believe a thorough document was a long one, until a colleague told her, kindly but plainly, that she had stopped reading Aminata's updates halfway through. This session teaches you to edit a document down to what a reader can actually hold in mind at once, rather than everything you know about the topic.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Identify unnecessary complexity that makes a document harder to process. e Cut a sentence or paragraph without losing its actual meaning. e Recognise when additional detail is helping a reader versus burdening her.
¢ Revise a dense first draft into a version a tired reader can still follow. 2.0 Main Content
A Document Too Full to Finish

Aminata Diarra coordinates supplier relationships for an import business in Bissau, and her weekly supplier updates had grown, over several months, into dense two-page documents covering every conversation, every minor delay, every small detail she thought might someday matter. A colleague finally admitted she had started skimming only the first few lines each week, because reading the whole update took longer than she had to give it.
The Mind Can Only Hold So Much

In 1988, the researcher John Sweller published a study in Cognitive Science describing what he called cognitive load, the amount of mental effort a person's limited working memory can handle at any one time. His finding was direct: when a document presents more complexity than a reader's working memory can process at once, extra detail, unclear structure, unnecessary qualifications, understanding suffers, even if every individual fact in the document is accurate. A technically correct document can still fail simply by asking too much of the reader's attention at once.
Editing for What the Mind Can Actually Hold
Cutting What Does Not Change the Reader's Decision

A detail that would not change what the reader does next, an exact time of a routine phone call, a minor administrative step that resolved itself, can usually be cut entirely without any real loss to the document's purpose.

Combining Related Points Instead of Listing Every One Several small updates about the same underlying issue are often more useful to a reader combined into one clear statement than listed separately as though each were a distinct concern.

Testing Whether a Sentence Earns Its Place Asking, of every sentence, what would be lost if this were deleted, is a fast, reliable test; a sentence whose removal changes nothing about what the reader understands or does next has earned nothing by staying.
Key Practices .
¢ Cut any detail that would not change what the reader does next.
¢ Combine related small points into one clear statement rather than listing each separately.
e Test each sentence by asking what would be lost if it were removed.
e Read a dense draft as a tired reader would, not as the writer who already knows the material.
e Leave in only the complexity a decision genuinely depends on.
A Worked Example: Aminata's Update, Before and After

Aminata's original weekly update included a separate paragraph for each of six suppliers, each covering every call, minor delay and administrative note from the week, regardless of whether it affected anything the reader needed to decide.

Her revised update opens with a single sentence naming the only supplier issue that actually required a decision this week, a delayed shipment needing an alternate carrier approved by Friday. The other five suppliers, all proceeding normally, are summarised in one line each. The update is now under half a page, and her colleague reads every word of it now, because every word has earned its place.
Common Pitfalls

Equating thoroughness with length is a habit that traps many careful writers early in their reporting practice, and the result is often a document so dense that a reader gives up before reaching the parts that actually mattered. A shorter document that a reader finishes serves her better than a longer, more complete one she abandons halfway through.
What Editing Actually Protects

Cutting a document down is not a loss of information. It is a decision about which of that information the reader's limited attention should actually be spent on, made by the writer instead of left to whatever a tired reader happens to notice before giving up.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to edit a document down to what a reader's attention can actually hold, cutting detail that does not change her decision. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where the same respect for a reader's limits shapes which communication channel you choose.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Choose one paragraph from a document you wrote recently. What could be cut without losing its actual meaning?

2. Think of a document you struggled to finish reading. What made it feel heavier than it needed to be? Practical Output: Practical Output One dense document edited down by at least a third, with a one-sentence note on what was cut and why.
References and Further Reading
e Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257 to 285.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed:
e Ecclesiastes 5:2, on letting your words be few.
e Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari 2977, on being given concise, comprehensive speech.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Choosing How to Say It

blocks.text: Introduction

Daniel Chirwa, who has low vision and relies on screen-reader-compatible formatting for most of his reading, learned early that the right channel for a message matters as much as the words inside it. This session teaches you to match a message to the channel that can actually carry it, rather than defaulting to whichever one is easiest to reach for.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
e Match a message's complexity and sensitivity to an appropriate channel.
e Explain why a rich channel suits an ambiguous or sensitive message better than a lean one.
e Recognise when a written channel is actually the wrong choice for a message.
¢ Choose confidently between a call, a meeting, an email and a chat message for a real situation.
e Adapt your channel choice for a colleague's accessibility needs. 2.0 Main Content
A Difficult Message Sent the Wrong Way

Daniel Chirwa works as a claims assessor for an insurance company in Maseru, and early in his career he delivered a difficult decision, denying a colleague's request to work a modified schedule, entirely by chat message, in a handful of short lines sent between other tasks. The colleague read tone into the brevity that Daniel had never intended, and what should have been a five-minute conversation became a week of quiet tension neither of them had wanted.
Not Every Channel Carries the Same Weight

In 1986, the researchers Richard Daft and Robert Lengel published a study in Management Science describing what they called media richness, the idea that different communication channels vary in how much nuance, tone and immediate feedback they can carry. A face-to-face conversation or a phone call is rich, able to carry tone, allow immediate clarification, and convey warmth alongside difficult content. A written message is lean, efficient for simple, unambiguous information, but easily misread when the content is sensitive or open to interpretation. Their central finding was that matching a message's ambiguity to a channel's richness, not simply choosing whichever channel is fastest, produces clearer understanding.
Choosing a Channel on Purpose
Reaching for a Rich Channel When It Matters

A message that is sensitive, likely to be misread, or carries real emotional weight belongs in a richer channel, a call or a face-to-face conversation, where tone and immediate clarification are available.

Reaching for a Lean Channel When That Is Enough A simple, unambiguous update, a schedule confirmation, a routine status note, is usually better sent through a lean, written channel that does not require real-time attention from either person.
Adjusting for a Colleague's Accessibility Needs

The right channel also depends on the person receiving it; a colleague using screen-reading software needs a written message formatted for that tool, while a colleague who processes spoken information more easily may be better served by a call than a dense written explanation.
Key Practices

e Match a message's sensitivity and ambiguity to a channel rich enough to carry it. e Use a lean, written channel for simple, unambiguous information. e Pause before sending a difficult message through a channel that cannot carry tone.
e Ask, rather than assume, what channel and format actually work best for a specific colleague.
A Worked Example: Daniel's Second Difficult Conversation

Months later, Daniel faced a similar decision, denying a different request. This time, he asked the colleague for ten minutes on a call, explained the reasoning directly, and left room for the colleague to respond and ask questions in the moment. The decision itself did not change. The colleague's understanding of it did, because the channel could carry what a chat message never could, the tone of genuine consideration behind a difficult answer.

Daniel also began asking new colleagues directly how they preferred to receive detailed information, in writing, by call, or in a short meeting, rather than assuming his own preference would suit everyone he worked with.
Common Pitfalls

Reaching automatically for whichever channel is fastest or most familiar, rather than the one suited to the message, is the habit that causes the most avoidable misunderstanding at this stage. A quick chat message is rarely the wrong tool because it is quick. It is wrong when the message it carries needed more richness than a few typed lines could provide.
The Channel Is Part of the Message
Daniel's difficult conversations have not become easier to have. They have become easier to have well, because the channel now matches what the message actually needs to carry.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to match a message's ambiguity and sensitivity to an appropriately rich or lean communication channel. This prepares you for Study Session 6, where every principle from this course comes together in one finished, tested report.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Think of a message you once sent through the wrong channel. What went wrong, and which channel would have served it better?
2. Name one colleague whose channel or format preferences you have never actually asked about. What would you ask? Practical Output: Practical Output
A short account of one real message matched to an appropriate channel, naming why a richer or leaner channel was the right choice.
References and Further Reading
¢ Daft, R.L., & Lengel, R.H. (1986). Organizational information requirements, media richness and structural design. Management Science, 32(5), 554 to 571.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed:
e 1Corinthians 14:9, on speech that is not intelligible being like speaking into the air.
e Qur'an, Surah Al-Bagarah 2:283, on trust and a verbal pledge when writing is not practical.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: From Draft to Something Someone Can Use

blocks.text: Introduction

Every session so far has taught one part of writing well at work. This final session asks Ndeye Fall, and you, to bring audience awareness, front-loaded structure, careful editing and the right channel together into one finished report, tested against a real reader before it is called done.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Assemble a complete report using the structure, editing and channel principles from Sessions 1 to 5. e Test a finished document against a real or imagined reader before sending it. e Revise a document based on where a reader actually struggled, not where the writer assumed she would.
e Submit one complete, reader-tested report with confidence. 2.0 Main Content
A Report Ndeye Was Sure Was Finished

Ndeye Fall coordinates community health outreach records for a clinic network in Nouakchott, and she was confident her quarterly summary report was finished, until she asked a colleague outside her department to read it and explain back what it said. The colleague's summary left out the report's actual main recommendation entirely. Ndeye had been sure it was obvious. It was not.
A Document Improves When a Real Reader Meets It

In 1997, the document design researcher Karen Schriver published Dynamics in Document Design, arguing that a document improves most reliably not through a writer's own repeated proofreading, which mainly catches what the writer already expects to see, but through direct testing with real readers, watching or asking where they actually get confused, lost or misled. Her central point was that a writer's deep familiarity with her own document makes her a poor judge of where a stranger will actually struggle, which is exactly why an outside reader catches what the writer cannot.
Assembling and Testing a Finished Report
Assembling With Every Earlier Principle in Place

A finished report should open with its main conclusion, as Session 3 taught, use only the detail a reader actually needs, as Session 4 taught, and be delivered through a channel matched to its content, as Session 5 taught, brought together rather than practised separately.
Testing With a Real or Imagined Reader

Asking one real colleague to read a draft and explain its main point back, or, when that is not possible, rereading it deliberately as a specific named reader would, often reveals a gap between what the writer believes is obvious and what a fresh reader actually takes away.

Revising Where the Reader Actually Struggled The most useful revision targets the exact place a real reader hesitated, misunderstood or stopped reading, rather than a general polish applied evenly across a document that may already be working in most of its parts.
Key Practices
e Assemble a report using structure, editing and channel choices together, not as separate steps. e Ask areal reader to explain a draft's main point back to you before finalising it.
e Revise the exact place a reader actually struggled, not the whole document evenly.
¢ Confirm the finished report still opens with its main conclusion before sending it.
¢ Choose a delivery channel matched to the report's actual content and audience.
A Worked Example: Ndeye's Report, Tested and Revised

When Ndeye's colleague missed the report's main recommendation, she traced the gap to its actual location: the recommendation appeared in a bullet list halfway through the document, formatted identically to six less important supporting details around it, with nothing to signal it as the most important line in the report.

Her revision did not shorten the report or add new content. It moved the recommendation to the opening summary, bolded it, and left the supporting bullet list unchanged beneath. A second colleague, asked to read the revised version, named the recommendation correctly within the first sentence of her summary. Nothing about the underlying information had changed. Its visibility to a real reader had.
Common Pitfalls

Trusting one's own repeated proofreading as sufficient testing is the assumption that trips up even careful writers at this final stage, because a writer rereading her own document is confirming what she already knows it says, not discovering what a stranger would actually take from it. A document is only truly finished once someone other than its writer has read it and confirmed what it actually communicates.
Finished Means Tested, Not Just Complete

Ndeye's reports now leave her hands only after someone else has confirmed what they actually say, not only what she intended them to say, and that single habit, more than any sentence-level polish, is what this course has been building toward across six sessions.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to assemble a complete report using every earlier principle together, and to test it against a real reader before calling it finished. This closes Course 71 and prepares you for Course 72, Meetings, Minutes and Team Communication.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Ask a real colleague to read one of your recent documents and explain its main point back to you. What did you learn?

quiz.q: Aminata's colleague admitted she had stopped reading past the first few lines of her weekly updates. What was the underlying cause?
options: The updates contained factual errors
The updates had grown too dense to finish reading in the time available
The colleague disliked Aminata personally
The updates were sent too rarely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Cutting It Down to What Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Sweller's 1988 research, what is cognitive load?
options: The physical effort of writing a document
The amount of mental effort a person's limited working memory can handle at one time
The total number of pages in a document
A measure of how fast a document was written
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Cutting It Down to What Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session identify as a risk of unnecessary complexity in a document?
options: It has no real effect if the facts are accurate
It can overwhelm a reader's working memory and reduce understanding even when facts are correct
It always improves a reader's comprehension
It only affects readers with less education
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Cutting It Down to What Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: Daniel's chat message denying a colleague's schedule request caused a week of tension. What was the underlying cause?
options: The decision itself was unfair
A lean channel could not carry the tone and nuance the sensitive message needed
The colleague never read the message
Chat messages are always inappropriate at work
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Choosing How to Say It) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Daft and Lengel's 1986 media richness theory, what makes a channel like a phone call richer than a written message?
options: It takes longer to use
It can carry tone, allow immediate clarification, and convey nuance
It is always the cheaper option
It requires no preparation at all
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Choosing How to Say It) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to this session, what type of message is well suited to a lean, written channel?
options: Asensitive, ambiguous decision
A simple, unambiguous update
Any message regardless of content
Only messages longer than one page
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Choosing How to Say It) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Zainab's finance team did not read past the first page of her memo. What was the underlying cause?
options: The memo used incorrect grammar
The memo buried its actual request under two pages of background the reader did not need repeated
The finance team was too busy to read any memo
The memo was too short
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Flower and Hayes's 1981 research, what do skilled writers do differently from less skilled writers?
options: They write faster
They hold an active mental picture of their reader and purpose throughout the writing process
They avoid revising their work
They use longer sentences
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend naming before drafting a document?
options: The writer's own opinion only
What the specific reader already knows and what the document needs to achieve
The longest possible background explanation
Nothing, drafting should begin immediately
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Who Is Actually Reading This) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Patrick's emails to drivers and warehouse staff often went unanswered. What was the actual cause, according to this session?
options: His information was consistently wrong
His actual request usually appeared in the third paragraph, after readers had stopped reading
Colleagues did not have email access
His emails were too short
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Nielsen's 2006 eyetracking study, how do people typically read on a screen?
options: Word by word, in complete order, every time
In an F-shaped pattern, with the first line receiving far more attention than later text
From the bottom of the page upward
They do not read screens differently from printed pages
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What makes a subject line effective, according to this session?
options: Vagueness, so the reader is curious enough to open it
Stating the actual request so the reader can prioritise it correctly
Length, the longer the better
Including as many topics as possible in one line
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (The Email That Gets Answered) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Rahel's early field reports read like a diary of her month. What did her programme director eventually ask her to change?
options: To include more daily detail
To lead with what the head office actually needed to know or decide
To stop submitting reports altogether
To write in a more casual tone
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (A Report That Holds Its Shape) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to the 2011 Federal Plain Language Guidelines, where should a document's main point appear?
options: Buried within the supporting detail
Early, ideally in an opening summary, before the supporting detail
Only in a footnote .
It does not matter where the main point appears
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (A Report That Holds Its Shape) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What is the purpose of using consistent, predictable headings in a report?
options: To make the report look longer
To let a reader find the section she needs without reading the whole report
Headings have no real effect on how a report is read
To replace the need for a summary
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (A Report That Holds Its Shape) before continuing.
